column4: Good soil yields by its Lord's permission, bad soil yields only scant growth, and the ayah closes with gratitude; this states the section's fertile-versus-kanud earth image almost whole.
The winds carry a heavy cloud to dead land, water descends, and fruits emerge; this is the nurturing sequence whose two soils are distinguished in 7:58.
The wind raises cloud with the exact secondary action فَتُثِيرُ سَحَابًا named from the source section, then rain issues from it.
Winds تُثِيرُ سَحَابًا and the cloud revives dead land, joining the section's exact wind-cloud wording to earth made productive.
The uncountability of God's favor is set against إِنَّ ٱلْإِنسَانَ لَظَلُومٌ كَفَّارٌ; it reverses the kenud who counts misfortunes and forgets gifts.
People recognize God's favor and then deny it; knowledge of the gift without preserving its relation to the giver is precisely the section's cut gratitude.
The human is asked what deceived him concerning his generous Lord, bringing the section's human, giving generosity, and forgotten Rabb into one address.
After God rescues people from danger at sea they turn away, and the human is called ungrateful; the rescue-to-forgetting turn enacts kenud.
God makes humankind testify against themselves to His lordship; Rabb and self-witness meet exactly as the section allows for the pronoun in 100:7.
After being shown the way, the human may be grateful or ungrateful; the ayah states the two possible returns to divine guidance.
The same formula إِنَّ ٱلْإِنسَانَ introduces the human's transgression, whose cause 96:7 identifies as imagined independence from care.
The human transgresses because he sees himself as self-sufficient, naming the illusion by which a recipient forgets the nurturing Lord of 96:6.
Good received is from God, while evil that befalls is from oneself, and God suffices as witness; this corrects the kenud habit of remembering harms but losing their gifts' source.
“Remember Me, I will remember you” makes the relation reciprocal, then commands gratitude and forbids ingratitude; it is the uncut version of the section's two-way cord.
Holding God's rope is joined to remembering His favor and the bond He made between formerly hostile hearts, a direct positive form of the section's cut favor-cord.
The command not to break confirmed oaths says that God is witness to what people do, combining an unbroken bond with the section's knowing witness.
The woman who unravels her yarn after it was strong supplies a literal cord-image for breaking a confirmed relation, continuing 16:91.
The Lord promises increase for gratitude and warns of punishment for ingratitude, showing that the receiver's return either continues or breaks bounty.
Solomon calls the gift “the bounty of my Lord” and a test of gratitude or ingratitude, then says his Lord is self-sufficient and generous.
A good land with two gardens is explicitly paired with “eat of your Lord's provision and thank Him,” the productive answer to the section's rain and care.
When the people turn away, the flood of the dam replaces their two gardens with bitter, sparse growth; severed gratitude becomes ruined earth.
The ruined gardens are called a recompense for ingratitude, making explicit what the flood-and-field reversal in 34:16 means.
God revives dead earth and brings grain, حَبًّا, from it; the source section explicitly hears this grain beside حُبّ in 100:8.
Gardens and flowing springs complete the watered field introduced in 36:33.
People eat the field's fruit although their hands did not create it, and are asked whether they will thank; gift, labor, and return meet explicitly.
The question “Have you considered what you till?” places the human farmer inside the section's field.
God asks whether people make the crop grow or He does, distinguishing the worker of the soil from the Lord who actually nurtures it.
God could make the crop shattered debris; this is the explicit non-yield boundary of the otherwise tended field.
The water people drink is called to attention as part of the gift-chain that makes their field possible.
God asks whether people send water from the raincloud or He does, identifying the cloud's nurturing agency with its giver.
God could make the water bitter and therefore asks why people do not give thanks; usable rain and gratitude are joined directly.
A gift spoiled by reproach is like soil on smooth rock stripped bare by rain; giving whose relation is cut produces nothing.
Sincere spending is a garden whose rain doubles its yield and whose drizzle still suffices, the fruitful opposite of both 2:264 and kenud soil.
Spending in God's way is a grain that grows seven ears and manifold seed, turning a passed-on gift into cultivated abundance.
The garden owners are tested through the crop they presume they can harvest, making cultivated bounty itself the site of their response.
A visitation from their Lord circles the garden while they sleep; the giver can withhold the growth the owners treated as theirs alone.
The garden becomes as if harvested bare, a vivid counterpart to land that gives nothing.
The owners agree that no poor person will enter the garden, cutting the onward path by which the received bounty should become generosity.
They proceed intending deprivation while imagining themselves capable, combining control of the field with refusal to give.
On seeing the ruined field they conclude that they are deprived, counting their loss after they had planned others' deprivation.
The most balanced among them recalls that he urged them to glorify God, naming the response to bounty they omitted.
They finally glorify their Lord and confess wrongdoing, restoring in speech the giver whom their plan had excluded.
They hope their Lord will replace the garden with something better and turn toward Him, explicitly reattaching field and giver.
The parable begins with a man given two vineyards surrounded by palms and crops, making cultivated plenty a received gift.
Both gardens yield fully without withholding anything and a river runs between them, the complete opposite of non-producing soil.
Possessing abundant fruit and wealth leads the owner to boast of being greater, showing bounty being mistaken for self-sufficiency.
He enters his garden wronging himself and declares that it will never perish, forgetting the giver while loving the gift.
His companion recalls the One who created him through stages and challenges his rejection, answering the owner's self-sufficient stance.
The companion declares “He is Allah, my Lord” and refuses partners, restoring the true owner behind the garden.
The owner should have entered saying that what God wills occurs and power belongs to God; this is the missing acknowledgment at receipt of the gift.
The companion warns that his Lord may give a better garden and send a calamity upon this one, locating both gift and loss under the Rabb.
The garden's water may sink so deep that its owner cannot recover it, a boundary to the section's water collecting accessibly in low soil.
The crop is destroyed and the owner wrings his hands over what he spent, finally regretting the partners he set beside his Lord.
A secure town with abundant provision responds to God's favors with ingratitude and is made to taste hunger and fear; provision and kenud are directly opposed.
Every favor people possess is from God, and distress makes them appeal to Him, identifying the giver whom ease later obscures.
Once God removes distress, some assign partners to their Lord, cutting the appeal-to-rescue relation stated in 16:53.
Their partnership is said to deny what God gave them, naming ingratitude as rejection of the gift's source.
In harm the human turns to his Lord, then after being granted favor forgets the One previously invoked; it is an exact ease-after-affliction enactment of kenud.
When harm touches the human he calls God, but after favor he credits his own knowledge; the gift remains while its giver is erased.
The afflicted human calls God in every posture, then after relief passes on as though he never called, severing remembered need from received rescue.
When mercy is withdrawn after being tasted, the human becomes despairing and ungrateful, reducing the whole history of care to the present loss.
When favor follows hardship, the human says the evils have left and becomes exultant and boastful, enjoying the reversal without returning it to the giver.
Favor makes the human turn aside while evil makes him despair, the same asymmetric memory of blessing and harm described for kenud.
The human never tires of asking for ٱلْخَيْرِ but becomes despairing when evil touches him, using the named word in a broader “good” sense while privileging affliction over bounty.
After mercy follows distress, the human says “this is mine,” appropriating a received gift and doubting accountability.
Favor makes the human turn away, while harm produces prolonged prayer; the two directions display the section's cut return.
When his Lord tests him by honoring and favoring him, the human says “my Lord has honored me,” reading lordship only through abundance.
When his Lord measures provision, the human says “my Lord has humiliated me,” counting restriction while failing to understand the test paired with 89:15.
The charge that people love wealth with immense حُبًّا closely restates severe love of al-khayr and explains why gift eclipses giver.
The human is described as anxiously unstable, introducing the two unequal responses to harm and good in 70:20-21.
When evil touches him he is frantic, the adversity-counting side of the kenud disposition.
When ٱلْخَيْرُ touches him he withholds it, using the named word for received good that neither becomes gratitude nor continues onward.
If God expanded provision without measure people would transgress; He sends it by measure and is fully aware of His servants, joining calibrated care to خَبِير.
A tasted mercy makes people rejoice, but an evil earned by their hands exposes the human as ungrateful; the differing responses enact kenud.
Distress makes people call their Lord in repentance, but tasted mercy then leads a faction to associate partners with Him.
Their association is described as ingratitude for what God gave, making the severed relation in 30:33 explicit.
Ships move by God's favor so that He may show His signs, which are recognized by every steadfast, grateful person.
People in engulfing waves call God sincerely, yet after rescue some only partly fulfill the return; the ayah ends by naming treacherous ingratitude.
Those in a ship call God with exclusive devotion, supplying the moment when danger reveals the giver.
After rescue they deny what God gave them, the cut return that completes the scene of 29:65.
People promise gratitude if God rescues them from dangers of land and sea, explicitly voicing the return owed for deliverance.
God rescues them from every distress, yet they associate partners again; the promised gratitude of 6:63 is severed.
God subjects what is on earth and the ships, and restrains the sky from falling, a sustained picture of the Lord's preserving care.
The One who gives life, death, and life again is answered by a human described as deeply ungrateful.
The command “do good as God has done good to you” states the onward flow of received bounty and forbids corrupting the earth.
Qarun credits his wealth to his own knowledge, forgetting that it was received and reproducing the section's love of gift without giver.
Steadfastness on the way would be met with abundant water as a test, making gathered water both provision and a measure of response.
The abundant water of 72:16 tests people, while turning from remembrance of one's Lord leads elsewhere; gift and forgotten Rabb form the fork.
The Lord finds the addressee in need and enriches him, a concise instance of nurturing care and completed bounty.
The former orphan who was sheltered must not oppress an orphan, so received care is required to continue toward another.
The former needy recipient must not repel the one who asks, preserving rather than cutting the line of provision.
The favor of one's Lord must be recounted, the direct opposite of forgetting blessings while remembering hardships.
God announces that He has given abundance, placing a great gift before the response commanded in 108:2.
Prayer and sacrifice are directed to one's Lord because of the abundance in 108:1, an explicit gift-to-giver return.
Mary's Lord accepts her graciously and makes her grow with a good growth, using plant language for the section's gradual divine nurture.
The prayer “have mercy on them as they raised me when small” uses رَبَّيَانِي for stepwise human nurture and calls for a return of care.
“Our Lord is He who gave each thing its form and then guided it” states the source definition of Rabb as forming something stage by stage toward fitness.
God created people in successive stages, a direct formulation of the section's حالًا فحالًا account of nurture.
The generous Lord of 82:6 created, proportioned, and balanced the human, spelling out the care to which the human is ungrateful.
Human formation through successive stages is paired with barren earth that stirs, swells, and grows after rain, uniting both senses of gradual nurture.
Parental gestation and rearing culminate in a prayer for help to thank God's favor upon child and parents, linking nurture to its proper return.
Maternal weakness and nursing are followed by the command to thank God and one's parents, joining sustained nurture with reciprocal gratitude.
God brings people from the womb knowing nothing and gives hearing, sight, and hearts so that they may thank, a staged gift ordered toward gratitude.
After proportioning the human, God gives spirit, hearing, sight, and hearts, yet little thanks is given; completed formation meets failed return.
The Creator who produced people and gave hearing, sight, and hearts receives little gratitude, concisely matching nurture and kenud.
Purification is explained as God's desire to complete His favor so that people may be grateful, using the exact completion-of-bounty sense developed for Rabb.
After listing shade, shelter, clothing, and armor, God says He thus completes His favor so that people may submit.
The Lord creates people, makes earth and sky serviceable, and sends rain that produces fruits as provision; recipients are told not to give His place to rivals.
Neighboring soils and gardens drink the same water yet differ in produce, clarifying how response can differ despite one common nurture.
God sends fertilizing winds, brings water from the sky, and gives it to drink while humans do not control its stores; the whole field system is received.
Water descends in due measure and is lodged in the earth, while God can remove it; this closely matches water collected and held in the section's low soil.
Winds arrive as good tidings before mercy and pure water descends, beginning the same cloud-to-earth care sequence.
The water revives dead land and gives drink to creatures, identifying rain as distributed nurture.
The water is repeatedly presented so people may remember, yet most respond only with ingratitude; rain and kenud meet explicitly.
Water makes earth green, and the ayah closes by calling God subtle and خَبِير, joining the field to the divine knower in 100:11.
God sends water and grows splendid gardens whose trees people could not grow, then asks whether another deity stands with Him; cultivation exposes the true giver.
On the day of disclosure, mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify to earnings, concretizing the human's unavoidable witness to his own conduct.
The human is a witness against himself even while offering excuses, supporting the human referent of “he is witness to that” in 100:7.
Hearing, sight, and skins testify against their owners, giving bodily form to testimony over denied conduct.
The offenders did not expect their faculties to testify and supposed God did not know much of what they did, exactly opposing the Rabb whose knowledge cannot be escaped.
Their supposition about their Lord ruins them, showing that severing acknowledgment never places them outside His knowledge.
Whether speech is concealed or declared, God knows what is within breasts, paralleling the hidden contents gathered before the knowing Lord in 100:10-11.
The Creator necessarily knows what He formed and is called خَبِير, linking nurture, ownership, and complete knowledge.
Even a mustard-seed weight hidden in rock, heaven, or earth is brought forth by God, who is subtle and خَبِير; nothing buried escapes the Rabb's knowledge.
Pharaoh asks whether “we raised you among us as a child,” using نُرَبِّكَ for nurture while falsely occupying the benefactor's place.
Pharaoh follows his claim of nurture by calling Moses one of the ungrateful, a distorted human version of benefactor accusing recipient that clarifies true lordship by reversal.
Those who break God's covenant after its binding and cut what He commanded joined enact the severing that the section pictures as a cut cord of gratitude.
Breaking God's covenant and severing what He commanded joined gives the covenantal form of refusing to maintain the bond.
God makes charity grow while effacing usury and does not love any persistent ingrate; growth through generous giving is set against kafur.
The righteous giver seeks neither repayment nor thanks from the people fed, setting a boundary: human generosity should not demand the reciprocal gratitude owed to God.
The spending of wrongdoers is like a freezing wind destroying a crop; cultivated value becomes non-yield through their own wrongdoing.
The pasture brought forth in 87:4 is made dark stubble, marking the limit and passing end of growth rather than kenud soil's refusal to grow at all.
After imagined crop-loss the speakers dwell on the cost they incurred, illustrating the kenud focus on misfortune; its meaning depends on the ruined field in 56:65.
Their conclusion “we are deprived” completes the loss-counting response to the failed harvest of 56:65.
The garden owner doubts the Hour yet expects an even better return from his Lord, treating Rabb as guarantor of gifts while denying accountability.
The garden owners make no exception in their oath; this plausibly marks presumed control over bounty, including the remembered reading that they omitted “if God wills.”
Love of accumulated wealth, fine horses, livestock, and tilled land is made alluring; the list gives concrete forms to severe love of al-khayr.
People do not attain full goodness until they give from what they love, turning intense attachment to a gift into generosity.
Fine standing horses are presented to Solomon, supplying the concrete al-khayr whose love he names in 38:32.
Solomon says he loved the love of al-khayr over remembrance of his Lord, a close verbal meeting with حُبِّ ٱلْخَيْرِ and forgetting the giver.
The person who gathers and repeatedly counts wealth embodies love of the gift and a distorted practice of counting, though the section's kenud counts afflictions instead.
He supposes his wealth makes him last forever, extending the self-sufficiency produced by counted possessions in 104:2.
Wisdom is framed as gratitude; whoever thanks benefits himself, while the ungrateful cannot diminish the self-sufficient, praiseworthy giver.
God needs no one and is not pleased with ingratitude, but approves gratitude, defining the receiver's two stances without making the giver dependent on the return.
People are told to spend from that over which God made them successors, making generosity a continuation of property first entrusted to them.
Those who spend and do not follow the gift with reminders or injury preserve its benefit, the relational condition illustrated by the soils in 2:264-265.
At harvest people must give the crop's due and avoid excess, making a tended field the source of an onward gift rather than possession alone.
The sky is promised as abundant rain in response to turning back, beginning a renewed chain of nurture.
Rain becomes wealth, children, gardens, and rivers, unfolding the completed favors for which the surrounding address asks recognition.
The people are asked why they do not expect due greatness from God after the gifts of 71:11-12.
Rain revives earth, creatures spread, winds turn, and cloud is held between heaven and earth; this lays out the field's whole administered ecology.
Water from the sky produces vegetation and clustered grain, giving another direct formulation of the cloud-to-grain sequence.
Rain makes earth's growth luxuriant until its people think they control it, then God's command leaves it harvested bare; possession forgets the true giver.
Water descends, valleys carry it according to capacity, and flood bears passing foam while what benefits people remains in earth; this expands the section's pooled floodwater into measured reception.
The earth is spread and everything is caused to grow there in due balance, describing a field fitted before it yields.
The stores of all things are with God and descend only in known measure, identifying the hidden source behind the wind and water of 15:22.
Water from the sky supplies drink and the vegetation on which herds feed, the first movement of the section's nurturing rain.
The same water grows crops, olives, palms, grapes, and fruits, completing 16:10's movement from rain to yield.
God's favors cannot be counted, preserving the section's reversal of a kenud person who counts harms and forgets benefits.
God sends water and revives dead earth, a concise direct parallel to land made receptive by rain.
The earth is made serviceable, water descends, and diverse plants emerge, showing the Lord fitting ground and provision together.
Humans and cattle eat the growth, making the field's yield provision and a sign for people of understanding.
God drives clouds, joins them, and piles them until rain emerges, expanding the section's cloud as the agent of plant nurture.
Even those asked who sends rain and revives earth say “Allah,” yet most do not understand; verbal recognition has not become a full response.
Winds are sent as good tidings and means to seek God's bounty so that people may be grateful, joining wind, gift, and return.
The effects of God's mercy are seen in earth revived after death, inviting attention to the giver behind growth.
Water sent from the sky grows every noble kind on earth, a direct rain-to-soil parallel.
Water is driven to barren land and produces crops eaten by livestock and people, closely reversing earth that grows nothing despite care.
Water descends, enters the earth as springs, and brings crops through stages before they dry, matching collected water and gradual completion while marking growth's limit.
Humbled earth stirs and swells when water descends; the same giver who revives it will revive the dead.
Measured water descends and revives a dead land, tying calibrated provision to the earth's capacity to yield.
Provision descends from the sky, revives earth, and accompanies the changing winds, another compact version of the section's field system.
Blessed water produces gardens and grain for harvest, joining rain to the source section's secondary حَبّ image.
Tall palms with layered clusters specify the mature yield of the blessed water in 50:9.
The crop is provision for servants and revives dead land, naming the field's yield as a gift rather than an autonomous product.
The earth is laid out for creatures, preparing the provision named in the following ayat.
Fruit and palms stand on the prepared earth as its received yield.
Grain, ٱلْحَبُّ, and fragrant plants repeat the source section's grain-sense beside the loved “good.”
Immediately after earth, fruit, and grain, humans are asked which favors of their Lord they deny.
Rain-produced growth pleases its cultivators and then withers, using the farmer's gaze to show that even successful yield is not self-sustaining.
Abundant pouring water descends from rainclouds, initiating a compact field sequence.
The water brings forth grain and vegetation, again meeting the section's حَبّ sense.
Dense gardens complete the rain-to-growth sequence of 78:14-15.
Earth's water and pasture are brought out, describing provision emerging from prepared ground.
The water and pasture are called provision for humans and cattle, identifying the yield's beneficiaries.
The human is denounced for extreme ingratitude before his formation and food are unfolded, making the following care the measure of the charge.
A question directs the ungrateful human back to the material from which God created him.
Creation from a drop is followed by proportioning, one explicit stage in the Rabb's gradual formation.
God then makes the human's way easy, continuing the sequence of fitted care.
Death and burial remain under the same giver's ordering, so dependence is not ended by imagined self-sufficiency.
God raises the human when He wills, completing the staged history that begins in 80:19.
The human is commanded to look at his food, shifting the charge of ingratitude into inspection of provision.
God pours water abundantly, the first step in the food's cultivation.
God splits the earth open, making the soil receptive to that water.
Grain, حَبًّا, is grown in the opened earth, exactly supplying the section's secondary grain image.
Grapes and herbage add to the yield of the watered soil.
Olives and palms extend the cultivated provision.
Dense gardens show the completed growth of the sequence.
Fruit and pasture name further forms of what the tended earth gives.
The whole rain-and-field sequence is declared provision for people and their cattle.
The Lord creates and proportionally fashions, one concise description of care moving a thing toward completion.
He measures and guides, adding fitness and direction to the staged formation of 87:2.
He brings forth pasture, applying the creating and guiding Lord's care directly to plant growth.
The Lord promises to give until the recipient is satisfied, setting divine generosity before the remembered gifts later in the surah.
The Lord's shelter of the orphan is a concrete stage of the nurturing history that grounds the duties in 93:9-11.
Divine guidance supplies another stage of care remembered before the command to recount favor.
The recipients are told to worship the Lord of the House, directing response to the owner behind the provisions in 106:4.
That Lord feeds against hunger and gives safety against fear, two concrete favors that explain the worship commanded in 106:3.
The Lord expands and measures provision with full sight and knowledge of His servants, joining calibrated bounty to divine awareness.
Tongues, hands, and feet testify to what people did, another resurrection scene in which a person cannot escape witness to conduct.
The skins answer that the God who gives all speech made them speak, locating their testimony under divine power rather than voluntary confession.
God knows what is concealed and disclosed and what breasts contain, closely matching the Lord informed of the contents brought out from within.
The described cow has not been trained تُثِيرُ ٱلْأَرْضَ or water a field, preserving the source section's secondary use of the same root for plowing.
God sends water from the sky, brings forth fruits as provision, and subjects ships and rivers; this supplies the cultivated gifts whose uncountability and human ingratitude 14:34 names.
By the measured water lodged in earth in 23:18, God produces palm and grape gardens with abundant fruit for people to eat.
The command to glorify the name of one's Lord gives the fitting response to the creating, measuring, guiding, and pasture-producing care of 87:2-4.
The first command is to read in the name of the Lord who created, identifying Rabb before the human's self-sufficient transgression in 96:6-7.
The command to read is repeated while the Lord is called the most generous, making 96:6-7 a rejection of acknowledged generosity.
God teaches the human what he did not know, completing the formative care that precedes the same human's transgression in 96:6.
God creates the human from a mixed drop for testing and gives hearing and sight, supplying the care to which 76:3 says gratitude or ingratitude answers.
Spouses, children, grandchildren, and good provision are given by God, yet people believe falsehood and deny God's favor; a whole history of nurture is cut from its giver.
God produces people and gives hearing, sight, and hearts, but little gratitude follows, directly pairing formative gifts with failed return.
Night is made for rest and day for sight, yet most people do not thank despite God's bounty to them.
God makes earth a settled place, forms people well, and provides good things, then identifies Himself as their Lord; ownership, fitting, and completed benefit meet.
Night and day are made for rest and seeking bounty so that people may give thanks, explicitly directing provision back toward gratitude.
Fresh and salt seas yield food and ornament, while ships cross so people may seek God's bounty and perhaps give thanks.
The subjected sea supplies food, ornaments, and travel for seeking God's bounty, and the sequence aims at gratitude.
Human creation begins from an extract of clay, opening a staged formation that parallels growth from prepared earth.
The human is then placed as a drop in a secure lodging, one distinct stage in gradual nurture.
Drop, clot, tissue, bones, flesh, and a new creation are formed in sequence, an especially full Quranic enactment of development حالًا فحالًا toward completion.
Creation from dust, drop, and clot proceeds through childhood, maturity, and old age, directly presenting the Lord's stage-by-stage formation.
People are created in their mothers through successive creations in three darknesses, then the ayah identifies this maker as Allah their Lord and sovereign.
Creation from a humble fluid begins a compact sequence of measured formation.
The fluid is placed in a secure lodging, showing protective nurture within the sequence.
The lodging holds it for a known term, adding duration and measure to formation.
God declares that He determined the process and is the best determiner, closing the staged womb scene with calibrated care.
God is said to have caused people to grow from earth as a growth, applying the section's plant image directly to divine nurture of humanity.
Abraham excludes the Lord of the worlds from the objects he calls enemies, separating the true Rabb from false claimants before listing His care.
The Lord of 26:77 is the One who created Abraham and guides him, the first stage of the care that defines true lordship.
He is the One who feeds and gives drink, making ordinary provision an ongoing act of the Rabb.
When Abraham is ill, the Lord heals him, extending nurture from provision to restoration.
The speaker asks whether any lord besides God should be sought when He is the Lord of everything, closely matching the source definition “the rabb of each thing is its owner.”
People are told to be rabbāniyyūn through teaching and studying scripture, a derivative of the named root that joins disciplined formation to divine learning.
Abraham tells his Lord that he settled descendants in an uncultivated valley, asks for fruit as provision, and states gratitude as the hoped-for response.
People are commanded to seek provision from God, worship Him, and thank Him, laying out giver, gift, and return in one ayah.
Believers are told to eat the good things God provided and thank Him if they worship Him, directly binding consumed provision to gratitude.
People must eat God's lawful good provision and thank God's favor, stating the response that kenud cuts off.
David's family is commanded to work in gratitude, and few servants are called truly grateful; gratitude is sustained action rather than mere possession of gifts.
People are told to remember when they were weak and afraid, then sheltered, strengthened, and given good provision so that they might thank.
Earlier peoples received abundant rain and flowing rivers but were destroyed for their sins and replaced, showing plentiful water as care that does not excuse refusal.
Seeking the Lord's forgiveness is followed by the promise of abundant rain and added strength, while turning away would sever that renewed relation.
At judgment the human is told to read his own record and is sufficient that day as reckoner against himself, a close parallel to self-witness in 100:7.
God has enumerated deeds that people forgot and will inform them of those deeds, then is called witness over everything; counting, forgetting, knowledge, and testimony converge.
Earth reports its news, turning the ground itself into a witness when hidden deeds are exposed.
Earth reports because its Lord inspired it, joining Rabb to the ground's testimony.
People emerge separately to be shown their deeds, specifying what the earth's report leads to.
Even an atom's weight of good is seen, so no return along the gift relation escapes disclosure.
Even an atom's weight of evil is seen, completing the exhaustive boundary of that disclosure.
The Creator knows what the human soul whispers and is nearer than the jugular vein, directly excluding escape from the Rabb's knowledge.
God knows every leaf that falls and every grain, حَبَّةٍ, in earth's darkness, joining the field's seed to complete knowledge of what is hidden.
A good word is likened to a good tree with a firm root and high branches, making stable relation visible as rooted growth.
The good tree gives fruit in every season by its Lord's permission, a verbal and conceptual parallel to the good land of 7:58.
God revives earth after its death immediately after warning against hardened hearts, inviting the responsive human to be read through receptive soil.
True righteousness includes giving wealth despite one's love for it, turning حُبّ of possession into an onward gift rather than kenud withholding.
The answer to what should be spent calls it خَيْر and directs it to relatives and vulnerable recipients, using the named word in an explicitly generous sense.
Whatever خَيْر people spend is for their own good and will be repaid fully, describing gift as a continuing rather than severed relation.
After helping others at the well, Moses tells his Lord that he is in need of whatever خَيْر He sends, recognizing good as a gift from its giver.
The rebuke after the two provision-tests says people do not honor the orphan, showing failed gratitude in treatment of another dependent.
They do not urge one another to feed the poor, so received provision does not continue outward.
They consume inheritance voraciously, preparing the charge of immense love of wealth in 89:20.
People will be questioned that day about enjoyed bounty, joining the loved gift to the knowing accountability it cannot escape.
The one who gives and is mindful embodies the continuing, generous response opposite the withholding kenud.
The one who withholds and considers himself self-sufficient combines the two central failures of the section: stopping the gift's flow and forgetting dependence.
Those summoned to spend from received wealth may withhold, but their stinginess harms themselves because God is self-sufficient and they are needy; turning away can bring replacement.
Believers are warned not to let wealth and children distract from remembrance of God, the precise boundary between loving gifts and forgetting their giver.
If family, acquired wealth, trade, and dwellings are more loved than God, people must await His command; حُبّ of gifts is measured against their giver.
After Qarun is swallowed, former admirers recognize that God expands and restricts provision and that His grace spared them, correcting their earlier fixation on the gift.
Turning away is associated with corrupting earth and severing kinship, a direct Quranic instance of refusing to maintain a relation.
